title: Automated High-Current Short-Circuit Test System for IEC 60898-1:2015 MCB Compliance.
org: Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution
description:
Background: The safety of electrical installations hinges on reliable Miniature Circuit Breakers (MCBs). IEC 60898-1:2015 mandates rigorous short-circuit breaking capacity tests, crucial for ensuring MCBs perform correctly under severe fault conditions.
Existing Problem: Current manual or semi-automated testing methods for MCBs introduce significant challenges. These include imprecise R (resistive) and XL (inductive) circuit configurations, increased test times, and elevated safety risks for personnel during high-energy fault current generation (up to 10,000A). This impacts test accuracy, repeatability, and overall safety in the MCB certification process.
Detailed Description: This proposal outlines an automated machine to precisely control test currents, voltages, and circuit impedance, executing high-current short-circuit tests on single pole, SPN, DP, TP, and FP MCBs (0.5A-63A) per IEC 60898-1:2015. It features an Automated R and XL Circuit Combination Module with high-power, automatically switched banks for precise power factor control. A High-Current Power Source (transformer-based) delivers up to 10,000A. The Test Station includes universal MCB mounting and a critical arc chute for safety A sophisticated Control and Data Acquisition System (PLC/Industrial PC) manages tests captures high-speed waveforms, and analyzes data (Ip, I2t). A user-friendly HMI allows parameter input and automatic report generation. Comprehensive safety systems are integrated.
Expected Solution: The automated machine will perform MCB breaking capacity tests with unprecedented accuracy and repeatability, fully adhering to IEC 60898-1:2015. This automation will ensure precise parameter control, significantly reduce test times, and enhance safety by minimizing human intervention during high-energy fault conditions. This state-of- he-art facility will provide a reliable platform for MCB certification, contributing directly to electrical safety and quality assurance.
summary: Innovation (2/5): draws on standard software/hardware techniques applied to a disaster management problem, placing it in the incremental band. Feasibility (2/5): as a hardware build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (4/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Disaster Management. Tech Depth (2/5): centers on compliance. Sustainability (2/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (1/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 13/30 -> Red verdict.

detail.title: Automated High-Current Short-Circuit Test System for IEC 60898-1:2015 MCB Compliance

overview.in_plain_terms: Build an automated test rig that safely and precisely puts circuit breakers through high-current short-circuit tests required for certification, instead of doing it manually with imprecise setups and real safety risk.
overview.why_it_matters: MCB certification protects everyone who relies on electrical safety devices. More precise, safer, repeatable testing directly improves the reliability of a product category everyone depends on.
pain_points: Manual/semi-automated testing has imprecise circuit configuration.
High-energy fault current generation (up to 10,000A) poses real personnel safety risk.
Test accuracy and repeatability suffer from manual variability.
overview.background: MCB certification requires precise, high-current short-circuit testing per IEC 60898-1:2015, but current manual/semi-automated methods are imprecise, slow, and pose safety risks to test personnel.
overview.whats_being_asked: An automated machine controlling test current, voltage, and circuit impedance for high-current short-circuit tests on a range of MCB types, with precise R/XL configuration and safety systems.
expected_solution: Automated R/XL circuit combination module for precise power factor control.
High-current power source delivering up to 10,000A.
Safe test station with arc chute protection.
PLC/industrial PC-based control and data acquisition system.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Incremental. This is industrial test-equipment automation, a well-understood engineering category, the value is in precision and safety engineering, not conceptual novelty.
analysis.invention_effort_note: Low as scored, but this significantly understates the real-world difficulty, this involves genuinely dangerous high-voltage/high-current electrical engineering (up to 10,000A) that is not remotely replicable at a hackathon for safety and equipment-access reasons.

competitive_landscape.note: Extremely specialized industrial test-equipment PS, essentially no hackathon team will have access to real high-current test equipment, this is close to unattemptable as a physical build.

innovation.note: Established industrial automation category, precision and safety engineering rather than novel concept.

invention.tag: Low on paper, but Deceptively Hard
invention.note: The scoring reflects component complexity, not the real barrier: genuine high-current electrical testing equipment and expertise.

technical_feasibility.tag: Not Achievable as a Real Build
technical_feasibility.note: Generating and safely controlling up to 10,000A fault currents requires industrial test-lab infrastructure, this cannot be built or safely operated at a hackathon venue under any circumstances.

impact_and_benefits.note: Genuine value to MCB certification labs and manufacturers, though a narrow, specialized audience.

architecture.note: Real safety-interlocked high-voltage systems, architecture that fundamentally requires certified industrial equipment, not hackathon-buildable hardware.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Red, and more strongly than the score alone suggests. The actual physical system described requires industrial high-current test infrastructure that poses genuine electrocution/fire risk if attempted without proper certified equipment, this is not a scaled-down-and-simulate situation like some other hardware PS, it's a hard safety boundary. Only viable as a software/control-system simulation, not a working physical build.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Extremely well-specified technical requirements (exact standards, exact current ranges, exact component types) if a team chooses to build the control software/simulation layer only.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Any attempt to physically replicate real high-current (up to 10,000A) testing at a hackathon venue is a genuine safety hazard, this must not be attempted with real high-voltage/high-current hardware under any circumstances.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: If attempting this PS, commit explicitly and only to a software simulation of the control/data-acquisition system, never a physical high-current build, state this safety boundary clearly and immediately in your pitch.

idea_0_4: Commit explicitly to a control-software and simulation-only build, no physical high-current hardware, ever, this is a firm safety boundary, not a scoping preference.
Design your simulated test-sequence logic based on the actual IEC 60898-1:2015 requirements described.
Split: one person on the control software/PLC-simulation logic, one on the data acquisition and reporting layer.
prototype_4_22: Build a simulated test-sequence controller that models the R/XL configuration and current-delivery logic described, entirely in software.
Build a simulated data acquisition system logging mock test results against the standard's pass/fail criteria.
Start a safety-interlock simulation layer, showing how a real system would prevent unsafe operation.
integration_22_30: Connect the simulated control sequence to the simulated data acquisition and reporting output.
Test your simulation against multiple MCB types/ratings named in the standard.
Build a clear pass/fail reporting output matching real certification report formats.
polish_30_36: Polish the simulation interface to look like a genuine industrial control system.
Rehearse being explicit and upfront from the start of your pitch: this is a control-software simulation, not physical high-current hardware, for safety reasons.
Prepare to explain what real deployment would require: certified test-lab infrastructure and safety engineering beyond a hackathon.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Lead with the safety framing immediately and confidently, a team that clearly understands why this can't be a physical hackathon build, and pivots smartly to the control-software value, will read as more credible than one that either avoids the PS or dangerously attempts real hardware.

strengths: Extremely precise technical specification available for building an accurate control-software simulation.
Very low competition, since most teams will avoid this PS entirely.
weaknesses: The core physical system is genuinely unbuildable and unsafe to attempt at a hackathon, a hard constraint, not a challenge to overcome.
Software-simulation-only scope significantly narrows what's demoable and may read as 'incomplete' to a judge who doesn't grasp the safety reasoning.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: Software-only team is appropriate here, no hardware/electrical engineering role is safe or necessary to attempt.
team_fit.approach: Research the actual IEC 60898-1:2015 standard requirements first, this grounds your simulation in real technical accuracy even without physical hardware.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: The control-sequence simulation logic and data acquisition/reporting UI, both standard software patterns.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Correctly representing the real IEC standard's test sequence and pass/fail criteria in your simulation, that requires actually reading and understanding the standard, not guessing.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: Presenting an AI-generated simulation as if it demonstrates a working physical testing capability, when no real hardware exists, would be a serious misrepresentation, especially given the genuine safety stakes of the real system.

data_resource_availability.status: No hackathon-accessible path to real high-current test equipment or data exists, this is a hard, non-negotiable constraint.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: There is no hardware backup plan here, the only responsible path is a clearly-labeled software simulation of the control and reporting logic.

judge_qna.question: Did you build a working physical test system?
judge_qna.strong_answer: No, and we want to be direct about why: safely generating and controlling up to 10,000A fault currents requires certified industrial test-lab infrastructure that cannot and should not be replicated at a hackathon, we built the control and data-acquisition software layer instead.
judge_qna.follow_up: What would a real deployment of your control software actually require in terms of physical infrastructure?

judge_qna.question: Isn't a software simulation missing the actual point of the problem statement?
judge_qna.strong_answer: The control, data-acquisition, and safety-interlock logic is a genuine, non-trivial part of the real system, and it's the part that's honestly buildable and demoable, we're not claiming to have solved the high-current hardware engineering, which is a different and much larger undertaking.
judge_qna.follow_up: How closely does your simulated test sequence match the actual IEC 60898-1:2015 procedure?
